what_it_does: In modern chips, power has to be delivered from the package pins all the way to the billions of transistors that actually do the work. This is done through a power delivery network (PDN) — a grid of metal wires that acts like the chip's electrical plumbing. Recent chip designs add metal layers on the back side of the silicon (backside metal), which can be used for either power wires or for signal wires that carry data. The problem is that traditional design flows claim the backside metal for power first, which boxes in the signal-routing step and forces signals onto less optimal paths. This paper proposes flipping that order: route signals first to minimize delay, then fit the power wires into whatever backside space remains. The paper argues this "PDN-last" strategy achieves better overall chip performance without sacrificing power integrity, and uses a fast analytical method to estimate how much voltage droops across the chip (called IR-drop analysis) to verify the power network is still adequate.
